content: The food composition database contains values for various nutrients, but some of these values may not represent true zeros (e.g., water content). However, this does not affect the analyses conducted. For Small Quantity Lipid-based Nutrient Supplements (SQ-LNS), no specific recipe is available, meaning the gram quantities or percentage-by-weight of ingredients are not provided in the specifications. The World Food Programme (WFP) specifications offer ranges rather than single values for energy and macronutrients. For these, values from Arimond et al. (2015) were used. Missing values for carbohydrate, fiber, and choline were imputed. Additionally, tryptophan values were imputed to calculate niacin equivalents. Carbohydrate: Energy from protein and fat was estimated using Atwater factors (4 kcal/g for protein and 9 kcal/g for fat). Carbohydrate energy was calculated by subtraction, and carbohydrate grams were derived using the Atwater factor of 4 kcal/g. Fiber: Peanuts were considered the sole source of fiber, while dry milk powder and peanuts were considered the only sources of protein, as information on quantities for other ingredients (e.g., whey powder, vegetable fat) was unavailable. Nutrient composition data from the USDA SR database (SR01091 for nonfat dry milk powder and SR16390 for peanuts) were used. Although the recipe for LNS is unavailable, information on the grams of dry milk powder is available (Kumordzie et al., 2019). Using this information, the following steps were taken: 1. The amount of protein from dry milk powder was estimated. 2. The amount of protein from peanuts was calculated by subtracting the dry milk protein from the total protein value in Arimond et al. (2015). 3. The grams of peanuts were back-calculated. 4. Fiber content was identified based on the estimated grams of peanuts. Choline: Dried skim milk powder and peanuts were considered the only sources of choline. Choline content was calculated by summing the choline from these two sources, based on the gram amounts of milk powder and back-calculated peanut grams in the SQ-LNS. Tryptophan: The tryptophan value was provided by a manufacturer (Nutriset, August 2020) to K. Dewey, a member of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), who subsequently shared it with the researchers. For Super Cereal Plus, the USAID document provided specifications for most macronutrients and ingredients as percentages by weight. Carbohydrate content was imputed by subtraction, using the specifications for minimum protein and fat percentages and maximum water, crude fiber, and ash percentages. To impute values for choline, tryptophan, copper, magnesium, and fatty acids, USDA SR28 values were selected for each ingredient, and the nutrient content of the ingredients was summed to derive estimates. Food Composition Databases: Various databases were consulted for food composition data, including primary USDA sources, global databases, regional databases, national databases, and project-specific databases. These databases were used to search for food composition data, even if they were not ultimately employed in the analyses. Outlier Analysis: Draft nutrient profiles were reviewed to identify undue influence from nutrient outliers within each food subgroup. Nutrient values were sorted from lowest to highest, and the following were examined: The range of nutrient values across all food items in the subgroup. The percent difference between the mean and median. The percentage of values excluded if a criterion of ±2 standard deviations from the mean was applied. The percent difference between the mean with and without exclusions based on ±2 standard deviations. Changes were made conservatively, as outliers may represent real and true values. However, adjustments were made when: Outliers were extreme and significantly impacted means. The source food composition database was less reliable. An item was a clear nutritional misfit within a group. In cases of high heterogeneity within subgroups, further division of the subgroups was considered. For example, liver from various mammals and birds consistently exhibited very high values for vitamin A and other nutrients compared to other organ meats, leading to the narrowing of the group to liver for modeling purposes. Similarly, seafood items showed high outliers for several nutrients compared to fish and were highly heterogeneous in nutrient content. Since fish were more widely consumed than seafood, the group for modeling purposes was narrowed to fish. Final Nutrient Profiles: After addressing outliers, final nutrient profiles were calculated as weighted means, with weights based on the number of countries reporting consumption of a given food item. Data were available for 38 countries. Nutrient densities (per 1000 kcal) were computed, sorted by macronutrient, fiber, and micronutrient density, and examined for each food group.
